procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 18.05.2011 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in CRLA No.202 of 2008
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court dismissed the appellant's appeal and upheld his conviction and sentence by the Trial Court for offences under Sections 302 and 307 of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant challenged the High Court's order in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the findings of the Trial Court and the High Court. The interim bail granted to the appellant was vacated, and he was directed to surrender before the trial court.

directions: The interim order dated 02.04.2012 granting bail to the appellant, hereby, stands vacated.
The appellant is hereby directed to surrender before the trial court within four weeks from today.
A copy of this Judgment shall be sent to the Trial Court to ensure that the appellant surrenders and undergoes the remaining part of his sentence.

issue.issue_text: Correctness of the order of the High Court upholding the conviction and sentence of the appellant for offences under ss. 302 and 307 IPC.

facts: The appellant was convicted by the Trial Court for offences under Sections 302 (murder) and 307 (attempted murder) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The High Court upheld this conviction and sentence.
The appellant challenged the High Court's order before the Supreme Court.
law: The appellant argued that his act should fall under Exception 1 to Section 300 of the IPC, which can reduce a charge of murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
application: The Supreme Court examined the evidence, specifically noting the nature of the weapon used, the number of gunshots fired at the deceased, and the part of the body where the shots were fired.
Based on these factors, the Court concluded that the appellant was determined to kill the deceased and that the act was unequivocally murder.
The Court explicitly stated that the facts of the case did not even remotely make out a case under Exception 1 or any other exception to Section 300 of the IPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the findings of the Trial Court and the High Court. It rejected the appellant's argument, dismissed the appeal, and upheld the conviction and sentence for murder.

issue.issue_text: Whether the provocation was grave and sudden enough to prevent the offence from amounting to murder is a question of fact.

facts: The appellant admitted to killing the deceased but argued that the act was a result of grave and sudden provocation.
The appellant contended that this provocation should reduce the offence from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
law: The court considered Exception 1 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, which states that culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, deprived of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes death.
The established legal test is whether a "reasonable person" from the same social background and in the same situation as the accused would have been provoked enough to lose self-control.
The fatal blow must be a direct result of the passion arising from the provocation, before there has been time for the passion to cool down.
application: The Court reasoned that provocation alone is insufficient to reduce the charge from murder. The provocation must be both "grave and sudden" enough to temporarily deprive a reasonable person of their self-control.

To determine this, the court must examine several factors specific to the case. These factors include the time gap between the provocation and the act of homicide, the kind of weapon used, and the number of blows inflicted.

The Court explicitly stated that these considerations are "all questions of facts." It further clarified that there is no fixed standard or test for what is a reasonable reaction in such circumstances, as this determination itself is "a question of fact to be determined by a Court."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, holding that whether a provocation was grave and sudden enough to prevent an offence from amounting to murder is a question of fact. This is because the determination requires a case-by-case analysis of various factual circumstances, rather than the application of a rigid legal rule.

issue.issue_text: Whether the practice of trial courts deferring cross-examination for a long period after the examination-in-chief is proper and does not affect the fairness of the trial.

facts: In the case before the court, a witness's examination-in-chief was completed, but the defense requested that the cross-examination be deferred.
The trial court granted the request, and the cross-examination took place more than two months later.
law: Section 231(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) grants a judge the discretion to permit the cross-examination of a witness to be deferred until other witnesses have been examined.
The Supreme Court's precedent in *State of Kerala v. Rasheed* sets guidelines for when such an adjournment can be given, emphasizing that a request for deferral must be based on sufficient reasons.
application: The Supreme Court strongly condemned the practice of granting long adjournments between examination-in-chief and cross-examination.
It reasoned that this practice is improper for two main reasons: it can affect the fairness of the trial and, in some cases, endanger the safety of the witness.
The Court established a general rule that, as far as possible, cross-examination should be conducted on the same day as the examination-in-chief or on the following day.

While acknowledging that Section 231(2) of the CrPC allows for deferrals, the Court clarified that this is not a right and should only be permitted in "very exceptional cases" and for reasons that are officially recorded.
The Court described the routine deferral of cross-examinations as an "unhealthy practice" that can seriously prejudice a fair trial and urged courts to be slow in granting such requests.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the practice, holding that deferring cross-examination for a long period is improper. It ruled that such long adjournments should never be given because they can compromise the fairness of the trial and the safety of the witness. The standard procedure should be to cross-examine a witness on the same or the next day, with deferrals being a rare exception granted only for recorded reasons.

cases.case_name: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: The fatal blow should be clearly traced to the influence of passion arising from provocation and not after the passion had cooled down by lapse of time, or otherwise giving room and scope for premeditation and calculation.
Under Section 105 of the Indian Evidence Act, the burden of proof that the accused’s case falls within a general exception is upon the accused himself.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Section 105 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the burden of proof is on the accused to establish that their case falls under an exception to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code. For the doctrine of 'grave and sudden provocation,' no abstract standard of reasonableness can be laid down; it is for the court to decide in each case based on the relevant circumstances, including the cultural, social, and emotional background of the society to which the accused belongs.
obiter: The court has reiterated in more than one case that reasons must be provided for its decisions.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the appellant's pleas of private self-defence and grave and sudden provocation were entirely unsubstantiated by evidence. The burden of proof for establishing such exceptions rests with the accused, and in this case, the defence failed to present any evidence to support its claims, leading the Court to conclude that the facts did not even remotely make out a case under any exception to Section 300 of the IPC.
legal_tests_applied: The burden of proof for a plea of self-defence is on the accused, who must present a reasonable and probable version of events; in the absence of proof, the court cannot presume the truth of the plea and shall presume the absence of such circumstances.
The burden of proof to bring a case under Exception 1 to Section 300 IPC (grave and sudden provocation) lies with the defence.
why_appellant_lost: The defence has not been able to establish a case of private defence by any evidence. There is no evidence on this aspect and therefore this plea was rightly rejected by the Trial Court as well as the Appellate Court.

The defence has not even been able to discharge its burden by showing that it is a case of grave and sudden provocation... There is however, nothing on record to show that the deceased hit the car at the gate...
The facts of the present case do not even remotely make out any case under Exception 1 to Section 300 of the IPC, or under any other Exception(s) to Section 300 of IPC.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the plea of private defence was unsubstantiated by evidence was affirmed by the court, which found a complete absence of proof for the appellant's claim.
The lower courts' rejection of the private defence plea was deemed correct because the appellant failed to meet the evidentiary burden required to establish it.
policy_considerations: The court noted its disapproval of the practice of trial courts deferring cross-examination for long periods after the examination-in-chief, citing precedents that address the fairness of trial procedures. (Inferred from the issue raised and the citation of cases like State of U.P v. Shambhu Nath Singh).
